summary: DMARC lets Domain Owners request aggregate reports from receivers. This Standards Track document defines those reports as an XML document with extensible elements, sent to the destination declared in DNS. It obsoletes RFC 7489.

plainLanguage.summary: DMARC lets the owner of an email domain ask receiving servers to send back a summary of how their mail was handled. This document defines that summary: an XML file listing each sending IP address, how many messages came from it, and whether the SPF and DKIM checks passed. It also defines how the file is named, delivered and secured, and how a server confirms that it may send reports to a third party's address.

questions: what is the rua tag in dmarc
how does dmarc verify external report destinations
subtitle: The XML file a mail server sends back to a domain owner showing how its mail was authenticated.

tldr.problem: A domain owner who publishes a DMARC policy has no way to see whether the policy is working, which servers really send their mail, or whether other people are forging their name.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines an XML report that a mail receiver sends to the address the domain published. Each record names a sending IP address, the number of messages received from it, the outcome the policy produced, and the raw SPF and DKIM results.
tldr.outcome: The report can carry extension elements, and the document defines how the file is named, delivered over TLS and treated when a duplicate arrives. It also defines a DNS check that confirms a receiver is allowed to send reports to a third party's address.

today: RFC 9990 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 7489, together with RFC 9989 and RFC 9991. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What an Aggregate Report Is For
sections.content:
A key component of Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) is the ability for Domain Owners to ask Mail Receivers for reports. These reports let Domain Owners see which IP addresses are sending on their behalf, and get some sense of whether the volume may be legitimate. The reports expose information about the DMARC policy, as well as the outcome of Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) validation.

The aggregate report is designed to give Domain Owners precise insight into authentication results, the corrective action they need to take, and the effect their DMARC policy has on the mail streams that receivers process. When Domain Owners can see what their policies and practices are doing, they are better willing and able to use quarantine and reject policies.

Visibility comes in the form of daily, or more frequent, feedback reports from Mail Receivers, containing aggregate data on the message streams relevant to the Domain Owner. This information includes data about messages that passed DMARC authentication as well as those that did not.

A separate report must be generated for each DMARC Policy Domain encountered during the reporting period, and each report holds data for only one policy configuration. Within one report there may be several records, one for each sending IP address and combination of results. The counts cover all messages received, even those whose delivery is ultimately blocked by other filtering agents.
sections.plainLanguage: When a company publishes a DMARC policy, the mail servers that receive its mail can send back a report saying which other servers sent mail claiming to be from that company, and whether those messages passed the SPF and DKIM checks. This document defines the format of that report, one file per domain per reporting period.

sections.title: The Structure of the Report File
sections.content:
The format of the report is defined by an XML Schema in Appendix A, and the document describes it element by element. Elements are marked for how often they may appear: O for optional, zero or one; R for required, exactly one; an asterisk for optional, zero or more; and a plus for required, one or more. Elements that hold text meant for humans may carry a lang attribute, whose default value is en.

The root element is feedback, in the DMARC namespace. Its first-level elements must appear in this order: an optional version, which must have the value 1.0; a required report_metadata; a required policy_published; an optional extension for future use; and one or more record elements.

The report metadata holds the reporting organization's name and contact address, optional extra contact information, a unique report identifier, the reporting period, optional error messages, and the name and version of the report generator. The reporting period is given as a date_range with a begin and an end, both the number of seconds since the epoch. These denote the reporting period rather than the first and last observed message, and reporting periods should not overlap; typically one covers a single UTC day beginning at 0000UTC.

The policy_published element holds the DMARC Policy Record found for the author domain: the domain itself, the method used to discover the record, the policy value, the subdomain policy, the failure reporting options, the DKIM and SPF alignment modes, and the testing flag. Unspecified tags carry their default values.
sections.plainLanguage: The report is an XML file. It starts with the version, then details of who generated it and when, then the policy that was found for the domain, and then one or more records, one for each sending address that was seen.

sections.title: Records, Rows and Identifiers
sections.content:
Each record covers one sending IP address for one combination of results. Its elements must appear in order: a required row, a required identifiers element, a required auth_results element, and any namespaced extension elements.

The row holds the connecting IP address, the number of messages for which the policy was applied, and the policy_evaluated element describing the outcome. That element holds the disposition that was applied, the result of the DKIM identifier alignment test, the result of the SPF identifier alignment test, and optionally the reason the policy was overridden. The spf and dkim values must be the evaluated values as they relate to DMARC, not the values the receiver may have used when overriding the policy.

The identifiers element holds the RFC5322.From domain, optionally the RFC5321.MailFrom domain the SPF check was applied to, and optionally the RFC5321.RcptTo domain. The envelope_from element may be present but empty when the message had a null reverse path.

The auth_results element holds the DKIM and SPF results as the receiver understood them, without interpretation by DMARC. If validation was attempted for any DKIM signature, the results must be included, within reason. Each DKIM result names the domain and selector used during validation, the verification result, and optionally a human-readable description. Each SPF result names the domain used, optionally the scope, of which mfrom is the only valid value, the verification result, and optionally a human-readable description.

When a message carries several DKIM signatures, some may pass and some may not. Signatures are listed in a preference order: first one that passes and is strictly aligned with the RFC5322.From domain, then one that passes and is relaxed aligned, then any other that pass, and last the ones that do not pass. A report should contain no more than 100 signatures for a given row.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record holds the sending IP address and the number of messages received from it, the outcome the policy produced, the domains the checks were run against, and the raw results of the DKIM and SPF checks themselves.

sections.title: Errors and Policy Override Reasons
sections.content:
The report may carry error messages about problems the receiver hit while processing the DMARC Policy Record, for example an invalid rua or sp tag, or several policy records at the same location. The error element is an unbounded string but should not hold an extremely large body; it should carry enough to help the Domain Owner understand the issue.

The reason element says why the applied policy does not match the published policy. It has a mandatory type element and an optional comment. The type must be one of five values. local_policy means the receiver's own local policy exempted the message from the action the Domain Owner asked for. mailing_list means local heuristics judged the message to have arrived via a mailing list, so authentication of the original message was not expected to succeed. other covers a policy exception not covered by the other entries, with details in the comment. policy_test_mode means the message was exempted by the testing mode, the t tag, in the policy record. trusted_forwarder means a failure of message authentication was anticipated by other evidence linking the message to a locally maintained list of known and trusted forwarders.
sections.plainLanguage: When a receiver does something other than what the domain asked for, it says why in a reason field, using one of five standard codes such as local_policy or mailing_list, and can add a free-text comment. Separately, an error field can carry messages about problems with the domain's own policy record, such as an invalid reporting address.

sections.title: Discovery, Delivery and Duplicates
sections.content:
A Mail Receiver discovers a reporting request when it looks up a DMARC Policy Record that corresponds to an RFC5322.From domain on received mail. The presence of the rua tag says where to send the feedback.

After preparing a report the receiver must evaluate the reporting URIs in the order given, ignore any that are malformed, and attempt delivery to every remaining URI up to its own limits. If delivery is impossible because the advertised service cannot accept reports, the receiver may cache the data and try again later, or discard it.

Unless the rua tag says otherwise, the report should be delivered over a channel using TLS, that is SMTP with STARTTLS. The message carrying the report must itself conform to the DMARC mechanism, so that it produces an aligned pass, which reduces the risk of a report consumer processing fraudulent reports.

The report itself is an XML file, which should be compressed with GZIP because without it the report may be too large for the receiver to process, and the total message size could exceed the receiver's SMTP size limit. The attachment must use the media type application/gzip when compressed and text/xml otherwise. Its filename is built as the receiver domain, then the policy domain, then the start timestamp, then the end timestamp, all separated by exclamation marks, then an optional unique identifier, then the extension, which is xml for a plain file and xml.gz for a compressed one. The timestamps are the number of seconds since 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970. A system that re-sends a report must use the same filename, so the receiver can overwrite the original or discard the second copy.

The subject line of the report message must have a fixed shape: the word Report, then Domain: and the policy domain, then Submitter: and the reporting organization's domain, and optionally Report-ID: with the identifier. The report identifier must be unique among reports sent to the same domain, so that a receiver can spot duplicates. A report generator may also use the same identifier in the Message-Id header.

When duplicates arrive, the decision is the receiver's: reject them back to the sender with a permanent failure, discard them, inspect the contents and act as appropriate, or accept them. Long-term duplicate data is not ideal.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver finds the reporting address in the domain's DNS record, sends the report by email, usually compressed, and names the file so the receiver can tell duplicates apart. The subject line carries the same information in a fixed form. Mail carrying a report must itself pass DMARC, so that forged reports are easy to spot.

sections.title: Verifying External Report Destinations
sections.content:
A DMARC Policy Record can point reports at a destination outside the authority of the Domain Owner that made the request, so that a domain that does not run mail servers can still have reports sent somewhere able to receive and process them. Without a check, a bad actor could publish a record that asks for reports to be sent to a victim address and then send mail that fails both DKIM and SPF checks to a wide variety of destinations, flooding the victim with unwanted reports. So a verification mechanism is included.

When the receiver finds a policy record in DNS and the Organizational Domain where it was found is not the same as the Organizational Domain of the host part of the authority component of the rua URI, the receiver must run a check. It extracts the host portion of the URI, prepends the string _report._dmarc, and prepends the domain the policy was retrieved from, converted to an A-label if needed. If the constructed name is longer than the DNS allows, the check stops without a positive result. The receiver then queries DNS for a TXT record at that name, and may fail the delivery temporarily so the check can be repeated if the query returns a temporary error.

The returned records are parsed as tag=value pairs in the same format as a DMARC Policy Record, and the v=DMARC1 tag is mandatory and must come first; records that fail this are discarded. If nothing survives the parsing, the check stops without a positive result. If at least one record survives, the external reporting arrangement was authorised, and a rua tag found in it replaces the one in the original record, so the report consumer can override the destination. The overriding URI must use the same destination host, which prevents loops and indirect abuse.

Where the check does not confirm the arrangement, the receiver must ignore the URI. If the confirming record points at yet another different host, the receiver must send the report to neither the original nor the overriding URI. A report consumer willing to receive reports for any domain can publish a wildcard TXT record at *._report._dmarc.example.com containing at least v=DMARC1.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain may ask for reports to be sent to an address belonging to somebody else, for example to a company that analyses mail for it. Because that could be abused to flood someone with unwanted reports, the receiver checks DNS for a record that confirms the arrangement before sending anything.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
A DMARC Policy Record can name an intermediary to receive reports on the Domain Owner's behalf, which happens when the Domain Owner contracts with an entity to monitor mail streams for abuse and performance issues. Whether a Mail Receiver may pass such data to a third party may or may not be permitted by the receiver's privacy policy or terms of use, and both Domain Owners and Mail Receivers should review whether their own internal policies constrain the use and transmission of DMARC reporting.

There is some potential for report recipients to perform traffic analysis, making it possible to obtain metadata about the receiver's traffic. Receivers need to consider that before sending reports to a third party.

The reports contain aggregated data relating to messages purportedly originating from the Domain Owner. The data holds no identifying characteristics about individual users: no personal information such as individual mail addresses, IP addresses of individuals, or the content of any messages.

Providing feedback to Public Suffix Operators for a Public Suffix Domain can, in some cases, cause information to leak out of an organisation to the operator, and that leakage could be used as part of a programme of pervasive surveillance. There are roughly three cases. For a single-organisation suffix such as .mil, there is no additional privacy risk, because the operator and the domain owners are the same. For a multi-organisation suffix that requires DMARC usage, such as .bank, reports are generated only for domains that do not publish their own policy record, and the only direct risk comes from domains that are out of compliance with the suffix policy. For a multi-organisation suffix that does not require DMARC usage, such as .com, the risk can be significant, because all feedback from domains that have not deployed DMARC is redirected to the operator, and the content of such reports is privacy sensitive.

Public Suffix Operators also receive feedback on domains that do not exist, which may resemble existing domains, and to reduce the risk, PSD DMARC feedback must be limited to aggregate reports, because failure reports carry more detail.
sections.plainLanguage: The reports contain no personal data: no individual addresses, no individual IP addresses and no message content. They do reveal traffic patterns, so sending them to a third party needs care. Reports about names under a shared suffix such as a country code domain can also carry information out of an organisation to the operator of that suffix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Aggregate reports are supposed to be processed automatically, so an attacker might attempt to compromise the integrity or availability of the report processor by sending malformed reports. In particular, the archive decompressor and the XML parser are at risk of resource exhaustion attacks, a zip bomb or an XML bomb.

The data contained in aggregate reports may be forged. An attacker might attempt to interfere with or influence policy decisions by submitting false reports in large volume. The attacker could also be trying to influence platform architecture decisions. A volume-based attack may also affect the ability of a report receiver to accept reports from other entities.

The availability of extensions could enable a report generator to disclose information about message placement, such as whether a message went to the inbox or to spam. This is strongly discouraged, because it could relay the information to a malicious party and allow them to understand more about the filtering methods used at the receiving organisation.
sections.plainLanguage: Reports are meant to be processed by machine, so a malformed report is an attack on the processor: a small compressed file that expands hugely, or a deeply nested XML file, can exhaust memory. The numbers in a report can also be forged to push a domain towards a stricter policy, and extensions should not be used to reveal where a message was filed.

viz.caption: THE ELEMENTS OF AN AGGREGATE REPORT

items.label: Local policy
items.desc: The receiver's own policy exempted the message.

items.label: Mailing list
items.desc: Local heuristics judged the message to have come via a mailing list.

items.label: Testing mode
items.desc: Exempted by the testing mode in the policy record.

items.label: Trusted forwarder
items.desc: Other evidence linked the message to a known trusted forwarder.

items.label: Other
items.desc: A policy exception not covered by the other values.

viz.caption: HOW A REPORT REACHES THE DOMAIN OWNER

messages.label: LOOK UP THE POLICY RECORD
messages.note: The rua tag in the domain's DMARC record gives the destination.

messages.label: SEND THE REPORT BY EMAIL
messages.note: An XML attachment, usually compressed, delivered over a channel using TLS.

messages.label: ACKNOWLEDGE OR REJECT
messages.note: Duplicates may be rejected, discarded, inspected or accepted.

viz.caption: THE REPORT FILENAME FORMAT AND AN EXAMPLE

data.title: Attachment filename
data.code:
filename = receiver "!" policy-domain "!" begin-timestamp
           "!" end-timestamp [ "!" unique-id ] "." extension

extension = "xml" / "xml.gz"

mail.receiver.example!example.com!1013662812!1013749130.xml.gz
